claim: Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative bacterium responsible for the human disease cholera.
source: Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative bacterium responsible for the human disease cholera (Nelson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nelson et al., 2009

claim: There are an estimated 3 million annual cholera infections, of which 100 thousand are fatal.
source: Estimates suggest 3 million annual infections, of which 100 thousand are fatal (Ali et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ali et al., 2015

claim: Most disease instances are attributed to the El Tor V. cholerae biotype, which is responsible for the ongoing 7th cholera pandemic.
source: Most disease instances are attributed to the El Tor V. cholerae biotype, which is responsible for the ongoing 7th cholera pandemic (Domman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Domman et al., 2017

claim: Over 1 billion people globally inhabit areas of cholera endemicity.
source: Globally, over 1 billion people inhabit areas of endemicity and future climatic change is likely to exacerbate the risk of illness (Ali et al., 2015; Asadgol et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ali et al., 2015 and Asadgol et al., 2019

claim: Future climatic change is likely to exacerbate the risk of cholera illness.
source: Globally, over 1 billion people inhabit areas of endemicity and future climatic change is likely to exacerbate the risk of illness (Ali et al., 2015; Asadgol et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ali et al., 2015 and Asadgol et al., 2019

claim: The success of V. cholerae as a pathogen is underpinned by an ability to colonise both aquatic ecosystems and the human intestinal tract.
source: The success of V. cholerae as a pathogen is underpinned by an ability to colonise both aquatic ecosystems and the human intestinal tract (Nelson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nelson et al., 2009

claim: In waterways, V. cholerae prospers by forming biofilms on arthropod exoskeletons.
source: In waterways, V. cholerae prospers by forming biofilms on arthropod exoskeletons.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text

claim: Degradation of chitinous surfaces ultimately liberates N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) for metabolism by V. cholerae.
source: Degradation of these chitinous surfaces ultimately liberates N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) for metabolism by the microbe (Meibom et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meibom et al., 2004

claim: Upon ingestion by a human host, V. cholerae express genetic determinants for acid tolerance, intestinal colonisation, and virulence.
source: Upon ingestion by a human host, V. cholerae express genetic determinants for acid tolerance, intestinal colonisation, and virulence.

claim: Diverse transcription factors regulate the transition of V. cholerae between environments and respond to signals including bile, temperature, nucleotide second messengers, and chitin availability.

claim: Quorum sensing is key for the transition of V. cholerae between ecological niches.
source: Quorum sensing is key for the transition of V. cholerae between ecological niches (Eickhoff and Bassler, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eickhoff and Bassler, 2018

claim: V. cholerae produce at least 3 autoinducer (AI) signalling molecules: cholera AI-1 (CAI-1), AI-2, and 3,5-dimethylpyrazin-2-ol (DPO).
source: Briefly, V. cholerae produce at least 3 autoinducer (AI) signalling molecules: cholera AI-1 (CAI-1), AI-2, and 3,5-dimethylpyrazin-2-ol (DPO) (Mukherjee and Bassler, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mukherjee and Bassler, 2019

claim: AI-2 and DPO are produced by multiple bacterial species.
source: Importantly, whilst AI-2 and DPO are produced by multiple bacterial species, CAI-1 is only made by other members of the Vibrio genus (Henke and Bassler, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Henke and Bassler, 2004

claim: CAI-1 is only made by members of the Vibrio genus.
source: Importantly, whilst AI-2 and DPO are produced by multiple bacterial species, CAI-1 is only made by other members of the Vibrio genus (Henke and Bassler, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Henke and Bassler, 2004

claim: V. cholerae can determine the crude composition of bacterial populations.
source: Thus, V. cholerae can determine the crude composition of bacterial populations.

claim: In the absence of their cognate AIs, when population density is low, the receptors for CAI-I and AI-2 target the transcription factor LuxO for phosphorylation via a phosphorelay system.
source: In the absence of their cognate AIs, when population density is low, the receptors for CAI-I and AI-2 target the transcription factor LuxO for phosphorylation via a phosphorelay system (Mukherjee and Bassler, 2019; Freeman and Bassler, 1999a; Freeman and Bassler, 1999b).

claim: When phosphorylated, LuxO upregulates the production of four small quorum regulatory RNAs (Qrrs).

claim: The Qrrs control expression of two global transcription factors: AphA and HapR.

claim: AphA production is activated by Qrrs.
source: Importantly, whilst AphA production is activated by Qrrs, synthesis of HapR is repressed.

claim: Synthesis of HapR is repressed by Qrrs.
source: Importantly, whilst AphA production is activated by Qrrs, synthesis of HapR is repressed.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text

claim: AphA and HapR control gene expression at low and high cell density respectively.

claim: HapR is a TetR-family member that binds DNA as a homodimer via a N-terminal helix-turn-helix motif.
source: Identified as a regulator of hapA, required for V. cholerae migration through intestinal mucosa, HapR is a TetR-family member that binds DNA as a homodimer via a N-terminal helix-turn-helix motif (De Silva et al., 2007; Jobling and Holmes, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Silva et al., 2007; Jobling and Holmes, 1997

claim: HapR is a regulator of hapA, which is required for V. cholerae migration through intestinal mucosa.
source: Identified as a regulator of hapA, required for V. cholerae migration through intestinal mucosa, HapR is a TetR-family member that binds DNA as a homodimer via a N-terminal helix-turn-helix motif (De Silva et al., 2007; Jobling and Holmes, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Silva et al., 2007; Jobling and Holmes, 1997

claim: Many clinical isolates of pandemic V. cholerae have lost the ability to properly express HapR.
source: Many clinical isolates of pandemic V. cholerae have lost the ability to properly express HapR and this may indicate adaptation to a more pathogenic lifestyle (Domman et al., 2017; Kamareddine et al., 2018; Heidelberg et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Domman et al., 2017; Kamareddine et al., 2018; Heidelberg et al., 2000

claim: Loss of HapR expression may indicate adaptation to a more pathogenic lifestyle.
source: Many clinical isolates of pandemic V. cholerae have lost the ability to properly express HapR and this may indicate adaptation to a more pathogenic lifestyle (Domman et al., 2017; Kamareddine et al., 2018; Heidelberg et al., 2000).

claim: In V. cholerae, HapR regulates the expression of ~100 genes to promote 'group behaviours' including natural competence, repression of virulence genes, and escape from the host intestinal mucosa.

claim: In Vibrio harveyi, LuxR regulates over 600 genes.

claim: CRP upregulates HapR expression.

claim: CRP is a regulator that controls metabolism of alternative carbon sources, including chitin.
source: In particular, cAMP receptor protein (CRP), a regulator that controls metabolism of alternative carbon sources, including chitin, upregulates HapR (Silva and Benitez, 2004).

claim: ChIP-seq was used to identify direct DNA binding targets of HapR and LuxO.

claim: At shared sites, HapR and CRP co-operatively bind offset faces of the double helix.
source: At such sites, HapR and CRP co-operatively bind offset faces of the double helix.
evidence: Stated as a finding of the study

source: Strikingly, this occludes a key CRP surface required to activate transcription.

claim: This mechanism allows V. cholerae species to integrate quorum sensing and cAMP signalling in the control of gene expression.
source: This simple mechanism allows V. cholerae species to integrate quorum sensing, and cAMP signalling, in the control of gene expression.

source: Previous work identified targets for LuxO adjacent to genes encoding the 4 Qrr sRNAs. We recovered all of these known LuxO targets, and an additional binding site was identified between VC1142 and VC1143.

claim: An additional LuxO binding site was identified between VC1142 and VC1143.

source: These divergent genes encode cold shock-like protein CspD, and the Clp protease adaptor protein, ClpS, respectively.

claim: Occurrences of the HapR binding motif were most frequent in the 200 bp preceding a gene start codon.

claim: Side chain E55 of CRP is required for stability of the DNA-CRP-HapR complex.
source: Both wild type CRP, and CRPE55A, were able to bind the murQP regulatory region similarly (lanes 1–4 and 10–13). As expected, HapR bound tightly to the wild type CRP:DNA complex (lanes 5–9). Conversely, HapR had a lower affinity for DNA in complex with CRPE55A (lanes 14–18). This suggests that the E55A mutation in CRP destabilises the interaction with HapR.
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 5d

claim: Residue E55 locates to a negatively charged surface of CRP called Activating Region 3 (AR3).
source: Residue E55 locates to a negatively charged surface of CRP called Activating Region 3 (AR3).

claim: AR3 aids recruitment of RNA polymerase when CRP binds close to the promoter –35 element.
source: This determinant aids recruitment of RNA polymerase when CRP binds close to the promoter –35 element (Rhodius and Busby, 2000).

claim: HapR reduced transcription dependent on wild type CRP by 50-fold.
